evals.prompt: I run a bakery in one town, about 300 Instagram followers. I have $150 total. What should I give away to get more local customers in the door?
evals.expected_output: Recommends the bakery's own product or in-store credit, redeemed in person, with several small winners or a repeat-visit structure. Explains why a broad prize would pull non-locals. Gives an estimate-labelled budget within $150 including any signage or promotion, two alternatives (one larger prize, a local partner bundle), a short adaptable description, and one next decision. Makes no entrant-count promise and does not cite the dataset as proof of results.
assertions: Preferred prize is own product or store credit redeemed locally
States why a broad-appeal prize suits this objective poorly
Budget lines are labelled estimates and total at or under $150
Offers two alternatives of different category or structure
Ends on a concrete next decision
Does not promise entrant numbers

evals.prompt: We sell accounting software for freelancers. Marketing wants to give away a PS5 to get sign-ups. Good idea?
evals.expected_output: Explains the reach-versus-relevance tradeoff: a PS5 attracts console fans and sweepstakes hobbyists, and the connection-to-business criterion fails. Says when it can still work (pure reach with a qualification step afterward) and when it fails (leads going straight to trials or sales). Offers on-brand alternatives such as a free annual plan, an accountant session, or a work-setup bundle, or a way to keep the PS5 tied to the product. States that the dataset cannot show which option performs better.
assertions: Names the audience mismatch and the missing connection to the business
Distinguishes the reach objective from the lead-quality objective
Offers at least two on-brand alternatives
States that the dataset cannot rank the options
Gives a keep, adjust or replace verdict
Where the aim is leads, prefers a Prize that only a buyer values and says the dataset holds no outcome after the entry

evals.prompt: Budget is $2,000. One $2,000 prize or ten $200 prizes? We sell running shoes online, want email subscribers who will buy.
evals.expected_output: Lays out the tradeoffs (headline value versus perceived odds, fulfillment multiplied, filtering for interest), recommends one structure with reasons tied to buyer intent, mentions a tiered middle option, and notes that the dataset's structure figures are descriptive only.
assertions: Compares headline value against odds and fulfillment cost
Recommends one structure and ties it to the subscriber-who-buys objective
Mentions a tiered or mixed option
Notes the dataset cannot show which structure performs better

evals.prompt: We're a 5-person B2B SaaS doing warehouse inventory software. Marketing wants to give away a MacBook Pro to maximise entrants, but honestly we would rather have 40 good leads than 4,000 randoms. What should the Prize be, and how do we judge it afterwards?
evals.expected_output: Gives a verdict of replace on the MacBook, since nearly anyone wants it. Offers at least two Prizes a buyer values and a consolation for qualified non-Winners

evals.prompt: We sell warehouse software and have a hard $1,000 total giveaway budget. The main Prize costs us $400 including delivery, and promotion costs $100. We expect 80 qualified non-Winners. We want to offer every one of them a printed stock-audit kit costing $8 plus $2 packing and $5 shipping. Can we promise that consolation, and what exact wording and budget should we publish?
evals.expected_output: Rejects the uncapped promise because each kit costs $15 all in and 80 kits cost $1,200, bringing total spend to $1,700 against the $1,000 limit. Reserves $500 for consolations, caps the offer at no more than 33 kits, and states how recipients qualify and how the capped kits are allocated. Gives public wording containing that quantity cap. Shows the chosen cap times $15, the maximum consolation liability and the complete campaign total including the $400 main Prize and $100 promotion. At 33 kits the liability is $495 and the total is $995, leaving $5. Any extra costs reduce the cap, and expected participation never replaces the public cap.
assertions: Identifies $15 as the all-in cost per kit, including $8 product, $2 packing and $5 shipping
Shows 80 kits would cost $1,200 and produce $1,700 total spend, exceeding the $1,000 budget
Provides public offer wording with an explicit cap of no more than 33 kits, eligibility and an allocation rule
Calculates maximum consolation liability as the chosen public cap multiplied by $15 and compares the full total with the $1,000 budget
Includes the $400 main Prize and $100 promotion in the full total, with any extra costs funded by reducing the cap
Does not rely on expected uptake or redemptions to bound liability
